newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FEATURE - Pakistan textile firm weaves a premier's dream.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Pakistan textile firm weaves a premier's dream.

text.p: Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif has a vision of export-led growth turning Pakistan from an economic weakling into a new Asian "tiger."
To ensure that this goal does not remain a dream, companies such as Mahmood Textile Mills Ltd will need to thrive.

Based in the city of Multan in the heart of Pakistan's Punjab province cotton belt, Mahmood Textiles is part of an industrial group with interests in spinning, weaving, tanning and farming, and a turnover of $80 million a year.

"We are exporting 98 percent of our spinning and weaving production," Khawaja Muhammad Iqbal, the director of Mahmood Textile Mills Ltd, told Reuters during a tour of his spinning and weaving factory near Multan.
He said Japanese buyers, who take about half the company's yarn output, had made meticulous checks before rating Mahmood Textiles as their top quality Pakistani yarn supplier.
Some yarn ends up, through Japanese traders, as denim cloth for jeans sold by retailers such as Britain's Marks & Spencer chain store.
"This means we have to have consistent good quality, so we are storing cotton for up to a year," he said ruefully, pointing to a row of warehouses piled high with baled cotton.
The cotton comes from seven plants operated by the group, making it Pakistan's biggest producer of ginned cotton.
PAKISTANI TEXTILES FACE TOUGH COMPETITION
Iqbal said the textile industry now seemed healthier after several years in the doldrums, but Pakistani manufacturers were finding it hard to compete with rivals in India and elsewhere.

"In India, our competitors are getting cotton at a very cheap price and selling yarn at a very low price in the Far East," he said. "This year we were purchasing cotton in Pakistan at even higher rates than the international price."
Iqbal said Mahmood Textiles had remained competitive despite high cotton prices because of investment in modern machinery and foreign demand for its high-quality products.
Nevertheless, he said the company was burdened by sky-high interest rates and electricity tariffs, as well as difficulties in finding and training a skilled labour force.

"Electricity is very expensive and there is loadshedding which affects production and spoils quality. So we are starting our own power generation plant, a captive plant only for our own units. Otherwise we will not be able to compete in the world."
The 9.2-megawatt Japanese unit, being built at a cost of 300 million rupees ($7.4 million), is expected to start production in August and lead to power cost savings of around 40 percent.
MOVING FROM RED TO BLACK

Mahmood Textiles achieved a net profit of 84 million rupees in the financial year ended September 30, compared to a loss of 45 million rupees the previous year, on an operating profit of 261 million rupees, against 79 million the previous year.
Earning per share was 12.71 rupees, compared to a negative 6.79 the previous year. The company distributed 15 percent bonus shares and a 10 percent cash dividend.
Iqbal said he expected this year's profits to be at about the same level as last year's, which he described as excellent.
The group's family sponsors have retained a 51 percent stake, with the remaining shares traded on the Karachi bourse.
Iqbal now plans to install 10 more looms alongside the 88 he already operates and move into finishing and dying to add value to the yarn produced on the company's 62,000 spindles.
"We have to have some collaborators for this as it is very sophisticated. We are looking for foreign partners and we are talking with them in Japan and South Korea," he said.
"If we don't go for value-added, then we can't survive."
